name: Crunch (Bodyweight)
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor, hands lightly behind your head.
Curl your shoulders up off the floor by contracting your abs.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The classic ab exercise — focus on curling the spine rather than pulling on the neck with your hands.
tips: Keep the lower back pressed into the floor throughout.
Exhale as you curl up to help engage the abs.
commonMistakes: Pulling on the neck with the hands.
Using momentum instead of a controlled contraction.
safetyNotes: Keep the neck relaxed and supported lightly.
Avoid jerking the head forward.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees bent, hands behind the head.
endingPosition: Shoulders curled up off the floor.

name: Bicycle Crunch
instructions: Lie on your back with hands lightly behind your head, knees bent and lifted.
Rotate your torso to bring one elbow toward the opposite knee while extending the other leg.
Switch sides in a continuous pedaling motion.
coachNote: Consistently ranks among the highest EMG-activation ab exercises since it combines flexion and rotation together.
tips: Rotate from the torso, not just the elbows.
Keep the movement slow and controlled rather than rushed.
commonMistakes: Pulling on the neck instead of rotating the torso.
Rushing through reps with poor rotation.
benefits: Trains rectus abdominis and obliques together.
safetyNotes: Keep the neck relaxed throughout.
Keep the lower back pressed into the floor.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees lifted, hands behind the head.
endingPosition: Elbow rotated toward the opposite knee, other leg extended.

name: Reverse Crunch
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees, arms flat at your sides for support.
Curl your hips up off the floor by contracting your lower abs, bringing your knees toward your chest.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: This emphasizes the lower portion of the rectus abdominis by moving the pelvis rather than the shoulders.
tips: Use the abs to curl the hips, not momentum from swinging the legs.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
commonMistakes: Swinging the legs using momentum instead of ab contraction.
Only lifting the hips slightly instead of curling the pelvis.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled, avoid swinging.
Keep the lower back supported.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees bent at 90 degrees.
endingPosition: Hips curled up, knees toward the chest.

name: Sit-Up
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet anchored or flat on the floor, hands crossed over your chest.
Curl your torso all the way up to a seated position by contracting the abs and hip flexors.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A larger range of motion than a crunch, involving more hip flexor contribution — a classic but more demanding ab exercise.
tips: Curl up smoothly rather than jerking upward.
Keep the feet anchored if flexibility or strength is limited.
commonMistakes: Using momentum by swinging the arms.
Anchoring the feet excessively, letting the hip flexors dominate the movement.
benefits: Full range-of-motion ab and hip flexor exercise.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled.
Stop if lower back discomfort occurs.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees bent, hands crossed on the chest.
endingPosition: Seated upright position.

name: Weighted Sit-Up (Plate)
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet anchored, holding a weight plate against your chest.
Curl your torso all the way up to a seated position, keeping the plate close to your chest.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Adding external load allows progressive overload once bodyweight sit-ups become too easy.
tips: Keep the plate close to the chest throughout.
Curl up smoothly rather than jerking upward.
commonMistakes: Holding the plate too far from the chest, adding excessive leverage.
Using momentum to swing up.
benefits: Builds ab and hip flexor strength.
safetyNotes: Start with a light plate to assess tolerance.
Stop if lower back discomfort occurs.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees bent, plate held on the chest.
endingPosition: Seated upright position, plate still on the chest.

name: Decline Sit-Up
instructions: Secure your feet at the top of a decline bench, lying back with your head toward the floor.
Curl your torso up to a seated position by contracting the abs.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The decline angle increases the range of motion and resistance compared to a flat sit-up.
tips: Curl up smoothly rather than jerking upward.
Control the descent rather than dropping quickly.
commonMistakes: Using a decline angle too steep before building adequate strength.
Using momentum instead of a controlled curl.
benefits: Increased range of motion and resistance.
Progressive step up from flat sit-ups.
safetyNotes: Ensure the feet are securely anchored.
Use a moderate decline angle to start.
startingPosition: Lying back on the decline bench, feet secured at the top.
endingPosition: Seated upright position.

name: V-Up
instructions: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight.
Simultaneously lift your torso and legs, reaching your hands toward your toes to form a V shape.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A demanding full-abdominal exercise combining upper and lower ab flexion simultaneously.
tips: Keep both the arms and legs as straight as possible.
Control the descent rather than dropping quickly.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees excessively to make the movement easier.
Using momentum by rocking the body.
benefits: Trains the entire rectus abdominis in one movement.
safetyNotes: Build up from easier ab exercises before attempting full V-ups.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Lying flat, arms overhead, legs straight.
endingPosition: Torso and legs lifted to form a V shape.

name: Hanging Leg Raise
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms fully extended, legs straight.
Raise your legs up in front of you until they're at least parallel to the floor, keeping them straight.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: One of the most challenging and effective lower-ab exercises — resist swinging by controlling the tempo.
tips: Avoid swinging the body to generate momentum.
Curl the pelvis under at the top for maximal ab contraction.
commonMistakes: Using momentum instead of strict control.
Bending the knees excessively to make the movement easier.
benefits: Highly effective lower ab and hip flexor builder.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
Build up with the knee raise variation first if needed.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar, legs straight.
endingPosition: Legs raised to parallel or above.

name: Hanging Knee Raise
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms fully extended.
Raise your knees up toward your chest by contracting the abs.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A more accessible entry point than a straight-leg hanging raise, building toward it over time.
tips: Avoid swinging the body to generate momentum.
Curl the pelvis under at the top for maximal ab contraction.
commonMistakes: Using momentum instead of strict control.
Only lifting the legs slightly instead of curling the pelvis.
benefits: Accessible progression toward a full hanging leg raise.
Effective lower ab and hip flexor builder.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar, legs extended down.
endingPosition: Knees raised toward the chest.

name: Lying Leg Raise
instructions: Lie flat on your back with legs straight and hands at your sides or under your lower back for support.
Raise your legs up together, keeping them straight, until they're pointing toward the ceiling.
Lower with control, stopping just before your feet touch the floor, then repeat.
coachNote: A floor-based lower ab exercise that's more accessible than hanging variations while still training the same pattern.
tips: Keep the lower back pressed into the floor throughout.
Control the descent rather than letting the legs drop.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor.
Dropping the legs quickly using momentum.
safetyNotes: Keep the lower back supported against the floor.
Reduce the range of motion if the lower back arches.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, legs straight, hands at the sides.
endingPosition: Legs raised toward the ceiling.

name: Flutter Kicks
instructions: Lie on your back with legs straight and slightly raised off the floor, hands at your sides or under your hips.
Alternate small up-and-down kicking motions with your legs while keeping them straight.
Continue for the desired duration or reps.
coachNote: A great high-rep finisher for the lower abs and hip flexors, keeping constant tension throughout.
tips: Keep the lower back pressed into the floor throughout.
Keep the kicks small and controlled.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor.
Raising the legs too high, reducing ab tension.
safetyNotes: Keep the lower back supported against the floor.
Reduce the leg height if the lower back arches.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, legs straight and slightly raised.
endingPosition: Same position, legs fluttering up and down.

name: Toe Touches
instructions: Lie on your back with legs extended straight up toward the ceiling.
Curl your shoulders up off the floor, reaching your hands toward your toes.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The vertical leg position provides extra hamstring stretch while emphasizing an upper ab crunch pattern.
tips: Reach toward the toes rather than pulling on the neck.
Keep the lower back pressed into the floor.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees to make reaching easier.
Using momentum to rock upward.
benefits: Combines an ab crunch with a light hamstring stretch.
safetyNotes: Keep the neck relaxed throughout.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, legs extended toward the ceiling.
endingPosition: Shoulders curled up, hands reaching toward the toes.

name: Cable Crunch (Kneeling)
instructions: Kneel below a high cable pulley, holding a rope attachment beside your head.
Curl your torso down and forward by contracting the abs, bringing your elbows toward your knees.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: One of the best exercises for adding progressive external load to direct ab training.
tips: Curl from the waist, keeping the hips relatively still.
Squeeze the abs hard at the bottom of each rep.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms instead of curling with the abs.
Using the hips to help move the weight instead of spinal flexion.
benefits: Easy to progressively overload the abs.
Constant cable tension throughout the range.
safetyNotes: Use a weight that allows full control.
Keep the movement focused on spinal flexion, not hip movement.
startingPosition: Kneeling, rope held beside the head, torso upright.
endingPosition: Torso curled down, elbows toward the knees.

name: Machine Crunch
instructions: Sit in the ab crunch machine with the pads positioned against your chest or shoulders.
Curl your torso forward by contracting the abs against the resistance.
Return with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The guided path makes it easy to isolate the abs with heavy progressive loading, ideal for beginners and advanced lifters alike.
tips: Curl using the abs, not by pulling with the arms.
Squeeze the abs hard at the bottom of the movement.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms on the handles instead of the abs.
Using a range of motion too short to fully engage the abs.
benefits: Guided path for safe, heavy ab loading.
safetyNotes: Adjust the seat and pad position correctly before loading.
Use a controlled tempo throughout.
startingPosition: Seated, pads against the chest, torso upright.
endingPosition: Torso curled forward.

name: Stability Ball Crunch
instructions: Lie back on a stability ball with your lower back supported, feet flat on the floor, hands lightly behind your head.
Curl your torso up by contracting the abs.
Lower with control back to the starting stretched position.
coachNote: The ball allows a deeper stretch at the bottom of the movement than a floor crunch, increasing the range of motion.
tips: Keep the hips stable on the ball throughout.
Curl using the abs, not by pulling on the neck.
commonMistakes: Pulling on the neck with the hands.
Losing balance on the ball during the movement.
benefits: Increased range of motion compared to a floor crunch.
safetyNotes: Use a properly inflated, stable ball.
Keep the feet planted firmly for balance.
startingPosition: Lying back on the ball, lower back supported.
endingPosition: Torso curled up off the ball.

name: Jackknife Sit-Up
instructions: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight.
Simultaneously lift your torso and legs, folding at the waist to meet in a jackknife position.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Very similar to a V-up, folding the body in half to work the entire rectus abdominis through a large range of motion.
tips: Keep the arms and legs as straight as possible.
Control the descent rather than dropping quickly.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees excessively to make the movement easier.
Using momentum by rocking the body.
benefits: Trains the entire rectus abdominis through a large range.
safetyNotes: Build up from easier ab exercises first.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Lying flat, arms overhead, legs straight.
endingPosition: Torso and legs folded together at the top.

name: Dragon Flag
instructions: Lie on a bench, gripping behind your head for support, and lift your entire body into a straight line except for the shoulders staying on the bench.
Lower your body toward the bench as a single rigid unit, controlling the descent with the abs.
Raise back up to the starting position without letting the hips sag.
coachNote: An extremely advanced ab exercise made famous by Bruce Lee — full-body tension must be maintained throughout the entire range.
tips: Keep the entire body rigid as a single unit throughout.
Lower only as far as you can control without the hips sagging.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag or bend during the lowering phase.
Attempting this before building sufficient hanging leg raise and hollow body strength.
benefits: Extremely effective full-abdominal and core strength builder.
safetyNotes: Build up through easier progressions like tuck or bent-knee dragon flags first.
Use a stable, secure bench with a solid grip point.
startingPosition: Lying on the bench, body lifted into a straight line, shoulders supported.
endingPosition: Body lowered toward the bench as a rigid unit.

name: Hollow Body Hold
instructions: Lie on your back and press your lower back into the floor, raising your shoulders and legs slightly off the ground.
Extend your arms overhead and hold the hollow, curved body position.
Hold for the desired duration, keeping the lower back pressed down throughout.
coachNote: A foundational gymnastics core position — mastering this hold builds the foundation for many advanced bodyweight skills.
tips: Keep the lower back pressed into the floor throughout.
Lower the legs only as far as you can hold without the back arching.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor.
Holding the legs too high, reducing the challenge.
benefits: Builds foundational core strength for gymnastics and calisthenics.
safetyNotes: Reduce the leg height or bend the knees if the lower back arches.
Breathe steadily throughout the hold.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, lower back pressed down, shoulders and legs slightly raised.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: Weighted Decline Sit-Up
instructions: Secure your feet at the top of a decline bench, holding a weight plate against your chest.
Curl your torso up to a seated position by contracting the abs.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Combining the decline angle with added resistance creates one of the more demanding progressive-overload ab exercises available.
tips: Keep the plate close to the chest throughout.
Curl up smoothly rather than jerking upward.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight before mastering the bodyweight decline sit-up.
Holding the plate too far from the chest.
benefits: Significant progressive overload potential for the abs.
safetyNotes: Master the bodyweight decline sit-up before adding load.
Start with a light plate.
startingPosition: Lying back on the decline bench, plate held on the chest.
endingPosition: Seated upright position.

name: Captain's Chair Leg Raise
instructions: Support your body on the captain's chair apparatus with forearms on the pads and back against the support.
Raise your knees or straight legs up toward your chest by contracting the abs.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The back support makes this more accessible than a hanging leg raise while still training the same lower-ab pattern.
tips: Avoid swinging the body to generate momentum.
Curl the pelvis under at the top for maximal ab contraction.
commonMistakes: Using momentum instead of strict control.
Leaning too far back against the support pad.
benefits: More accessible than a hanging leg raise.
safetyNotes: Adjust the pad height correctly before starting.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Supported on the apparatus, legs hanging straight down.
endingPosition: Knees or legs raised toward the chest.

name: Russian Twist
instructions: Sit on the floor with knees bent, leaning back slightly to engage the core, feet flat or lifted for more difficulty.
Rotate your torso to tap the floor on one side, then rotate to the other side.
Continue alternating sides for the desired reps.
coachNote: Lifting the feet off the floor significantly increases the difficulty by removing a stable base.
tips: Rotate from the torso, not just the arms.
Keep the chest up and back relatively straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back excessively.
Moving only the arms instead of rotating the torso.
benefits: Effective oblique and rotational core builder.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled, avoid rushing.
Lower the feet to the floor if balance is too difficult.
startingPosition: Seated, knees bent, leaning back slightly.
endingPosition: Torso rotated to tap the floor on one side.

name: Weighted Russian Twist
instructions: Sit on the floor with knees bent, leaning back slightly, holding a dumbbell or plate with both hands.
Rotate your torso to bring the weight to one side near the floor, then rotate to the other side.
Continue alternating sides for the desired reps.
coachNote: Adding load allows progressive overload for the obliques once the bodyweight version becomes too easy.
tips: Rotate from the torso, not just the arms.
Keep the chest up throughout the movement.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back excessively.
Using a weight too heavy to control with proper rotation.
benefits: Allows progressive overload for the obliques.
safetyNotes: Start with a light weight to assess tolerance.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Seated, knees bent, weight held with both hands.
endingPosition: Torso rotated with the weight brought to one side.

name: Dumbbell Side Bend
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in one hand at your side, other hand behind your head or on your hip.
Bend directly sideways at the waist toward the weighted side, lowering the dumbbell along your leg.
Return to standing by contracting the obliques on the opposite side, then repeat before switching sides.
coachNote: Use a moderate weight — very heavy loading here can build oblique bulk that can widen the waist appearance for some lifters.
tips: Bend directly sideways, not forward or backward.
Move through a controlled, deliberate range of motion.
commonMistakes: Twisting the torso instead of bending directly sideways.
Using momentum to swing the weight.
benefits: Simple to set up with a single dumbbell.
safetyNotes: Use a moderate weight to protect the spine.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbell in one hand.
endingPosition: Bent sideways toward the weighted side.

name: Cable Woodchopper (High to Low)
instructions: Stand sideways to a high cable pulley, gripping the handle with both hands.
Pull the handle diagonally down and across your body toward the opposite hip, rotating the torso.
Return with control to the starting position, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: This mimics the rotational, diagonal power pattern used in many sports, from swinging a bat to throwing a punch.
tips: Rotate through the torso and hips, not just the arms.
Keep the arms relatively straight, letting the core drive the motion.
commonMistakes: Using only the arms to pull instead of rotating the torso.
Using a weight too heavy to control the rotation properly.
benefits: Builds rotational power relevant to many sports.
Trains the obliques through a functional diagonal pattern.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo, especially when starting out.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing sideways to the machine, handle held high.
endingPosition: Handle pulled down and across to the opposite hip.

name: Cable Woodchopper (Low to High)
instructions: Stand sideways to a low cable pulley, gripping the handle with both hands.
Pull the handle diagonally up and across your body above the opposite shoulder, rotating the torso.
Return with control to the starting position, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: The upward diagonal pattern trains rotational power in the opposite direction to the high-to-low variation.
tips: Rotate through the torso and hips, not just the arms.
Pivot the back foot naturally as you rotate.
commonMistakes: Using only the arms to pull instead of rotating the torso.
Using a weight too heavy to control the rotation properly.
benefits: Builds rotational power relevant to many sports.
Complements the high-to-low pattern for complete rotational training.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo, especially when starting out.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing sideways to the machine, handle held low.
endingPosition: Handle pulled up and across above the opposite shoulder.

name: Standing Cable Side Bend
instructions: Stand sideways to a low cable pulley, holding the handle at your side.
Bend sideways away from the machine, allowing the obliques on the working side to stretch.
Contract the obliques to return to standing, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Cable resistance provides constant tension throughout the bend, unlike a dumbbell which loses tension near the top.
tips: Bend directly sideways, not forward or backward.
Move through a controlled, deliberate range of motion.
commonMistakes: Twisting the torso instead of bending directly sideways.
Using a weight too heavy to control properly.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the range of motion.
safetyNotes: Use a moderate weight to protect the spine.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
startingPosition: Standing sideways to the machine, handle at the side.
endingPosition: Bent sideways away from the machine.

name: Side Plank
instructions: Lie on your side, propped up on your forearm with elbow under the shoulder, legs stacked and straight.
Raise your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight line from head to feet.
Hold the position for the desired duration, then switch sides.
coachNote: A foundational anti-lateral-flexion exercise, training the obliques to resist side-bending forces rather than create movement.
tips: Keep the body in a straight line throughout, avoid sagging hips.
Stack the feet or stagger them for more stability.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
Rotating the torso forward or backward instead of staying stacked.
benefits: Builds oblique and lateral core stability.
safetyNotes: Use a pad under the elbow if on a hard floor.
Reduce the hold time if form begins to break down.
startingPosition: Side-lying, propped on the forearm, legs stacked.
endingPosition: Hips raised into a straight line, held statically for time.

name: Side Plank with Rotation
instructions: Start in a side plank position, propped on your forearm, top arm extended toward the ceiling.
Rotate your torso to thread the top arm underneath your body, then rotate back to the starting position.
Continue for the desired reps, then switch sides.
coachNote: Adding dynamic rotation on top of the static side plank position increases the oblique training demand significantly.
tips: Keep the hips elevated throughout the entire movement.
Rotate with control rather than swinging the arm.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips drop during the rotation.
Rushing through the movement.
benefits: Combines static stability with dynamic rotation.
safetyNotes: Master the standard side plank before adding rotation.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Side plank position, top arm extended toward the ceiling.
endingPosition: Top arm threaded underneath the body.

name: Landmine Rotation (Twist)
instructions: Stand holding the sleeve end of a landmine-anchored barbell with both hands, arms extended in front of you.
Rotate the bar from side to side, letting your hips and torso rotate together with control.
Continue alternating sides for the desired reps.
coachNote: The landmine's arcing path provides a natural, joint-friendly rotational pattern that's easy to load progressively.
tips: Let the hips and torso rotate together, not just the arms.
Keep the arms relatively straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Only moving the arms without rotating the torso and hips.
Using a weight too heavy to control the rotation smoothly.
benefits: Builds rotational core strength and power.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end firmly in the landmine attachment.
Start light while learning the pattern.
startingPosition: Standing, bar held with both hands extended forward.
endingPosition: Bar rotated to one side, hips and torso turned.

name: Hanging Oblique Raise
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms fully extended, legs straight.
Raise your legs up and to one side, bringing your knees toward that shoulder.
Lower with control back to the starting position, then repeat to the other side or alternate.
coachNote: An advanced progression from a hanging leg raise that adds a strong rotational and oblique component.
tips: Avoid swinging the body to generate momentum.
Control both the raise and the lowering phase.
commonMistakes: Using momentum instead of strict control.
Only rotating slightly instead of bringing the knees fully to the side.
benefits: Highly effective oblique and lower ab builder.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
Master the standard hanging leg raise first.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar, legs straight.
endingPosition: Legs raised and rotated to one side.

name: Windshield Wipers (Lying)
instructions: Lie on your back with arms extended out to the sides for stability, legs raised straight up toward the ceiling.
Rotate your legs together down to one side, keeping the shoulders flat on the floor.
Bring the legs back to center and rotate to the other side, continuing to alternate.
coachNote: A demanding oblique exercise that requires significant hip flexor flexibility and ab strength — regress with bent knees if needed.
tips: Keep the shoulders flat on the floor throughout.
Bend the knees to reduce difficulty if needed.
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders lift off the floor.
Dropping the legs too fast, using momentum.
benefits: Highly effective oblique and rotational core builder.
safetyNotes: Build up with bent knees before attempting straight legs.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, legs raised toward the ceiling, arms out to the sides.
endingPosition: Legs rotated down to one side, shoulders flat.

name: Oblique Crunch (Bodyweight)
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent and dropped to one side, hands lightly behind your head.
Curl your shoulders up off the floor by contracting the obliques.
Lower with control back to the starting position, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Dropping the knees to one side biases the crunch toward the obliques rather than a straight rectus abdominis contraction.
tips: Keep the lower back pressed into the floor throughout.
Avoid pulling on the neck with the hands.
commonMistakes: Pulling on the neck instead of curling with the obliques.
Using momentum instead of a controlled contraction.
safetyNotes: Keep the neck relaxed and supported lightly.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees bent and dropped to one side.
endingPosition: Shoulders curled up off the floor.

name: Medicine Ball Side Throw
instructions: Stand sideways to a solid wall, holding a medicine ball at your hip with both hands.
Rotate your torso away from the wall to load up, then explosively rotate back and throw the ball against the wall.
Catch the rebound if training with a bounce-back ball, or retrieve it, and repeat before switching sides.
coachNote: This trains the obliques for explosive power output, which is highly transferable to throwing, striking, and swinging sports.
tips: Generate power from the hips and torso, not just the arms.
Use a ball weight that allows a fast, explosive throw.
commonMistakes: Using a ball too heavy, slowing down the throw and reducing power development.
Only using the arms to throw instead of rotating the hips and torso.
benefits: Highly transferable to throwing and striking sports.
safetyNotes: Use a solid, appropriate wall or partner for throwing.
Warm up the torso and hips before explosive throws.
startingPosition: Standing sideways to the wall, ball at the hip, torso rotated away.
endingPosition: Ball thrown against the wall after rotating through.

name: Suitcase Carry
instructions: Stand holding a single heavy dumbbell in one hand at your side, like carrying a suitcase.
Walk forward for the desired distance while keeping your torso upright and resisting the pull of the weight to one side.
Switch hands and repeat for even training.
coachNote: This is a classic anti-lateral-flexion exercise — the goal is to resist leaning toward the weighted side, training the obliques isometrically.
tips: Keep the torso upright and resist leaning toward the weight.
Take controlled, even steps throughout.
commonMistakes: Leaning the torso toward the weighted side.
Using a weight too heavy to maintain an upright posture.
benefits: Also trains grip and postural strength.
safetyNotes: Keep the core braced throughout the carry.
Choose a weight that allows maintaining upright posture.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbell held at one side.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining an upright torso.

name: Plank (Forearm)
instructions: Get into a forearm plank position with elbows under the shoulders and body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core and hold the position, keeping the hips level.
Hold for the desired duration, breathing steadily throughout.
coachNote: The foundational anti-extension core exercise — the goal is to resist the lower back from sagging, not to hold as long as possible with poor form.
tips: Squeeze the glutes and brace the abs to keep the hips level.
Keep the neck neutral, looking at the floor.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
Raising the hips too high, reducing the core demand.
benefits: Builds foundational core stability and anti-extension strength.
safetyNotes: Stop if the lower back begins to ache or sag.
Use a pad under the elbows if on a hard floor.
startingPosition: Forearm plank, body in a straight line.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: Plank with Shoulder Tap
instructions: Start in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders, body in a straight line.
Lift one hand to tap the opposite shoulder, keeping the hips as still and level as possible.
Return the hand to the floor and repeat with the other side, continuing to alternate.
coachNote: This is an anti-rotation exercise — success means keeping the hips from rocking side to side as you tap, not tapping quickly.
tips: Keep the hips as still as possible throughout.
Widen the foot stance slightly for more stability if needed.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rock side to side with each tap.
Rushing through reps instead of controlling the anti-rotation.
safetyNotes: Master a standard plank hold before adding shoulder taps.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: High plank position, hands under the shoulders.
endingPosition: One hand tapping the opposite shoulder.

name: Pallof Press
instructions: Stand sideways to a cable pulley set at chest height, holding the handle with both hands at your chest.
Press the handle straight out in front of you, resisting the cable's pull to rotate your torso.
Return the handle to your chest with control, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: One of the best anti-rotation exercises available — the cable's lateral pull constantly tries to rotate you, and your job is to resist it.
tips: Keep the hips and shoulders square to the front throughout.
Press straight out, not toward the machine.
commonMistakes: Allowing the torso to rotate toward the machine.
Using a weight too heavy to resist rotation properly.
safetyNotes: Start with a light weight to learn the anti-rotation pattern.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing sideways to the machine, handle at the chest.
endingPosition: Handle pressed straight out in front, torso square.

name: Half-Kneeling Pallof Press
instructions: Kneel sideways to a cable pulley set at chest height in a half-kneeling position, holding the handle at your chest.
Press the handle straight out in front of you, resisting the cable's pull to rotate your torso.
Return the handle to your chest with control, then complete reps before switching sides and legs.
coachNote: The half-kneeling position removes the ability to use the legs for stability, increasing the demand on the core and hips.
tips: Keep the hips square to the front throughout.
Press straight out, not toward the machine.
commonMistakes: Allowing the torso or hips to rotate toward the machine.
Losing balance in the half-kneeling position.
benefits: Increased core and hip stability demand.
safetyNotes: Master the standing Pallof press first.
Use a pad under the kneeling knee if needed.
startingPosition: Half-kneeling, sideways to the machine, handle at the chest.
endingPosition: Handle pressed straight out in front, torso square.

name: Dead Bug
instructions: Lie on your back with arms extended toward the ceiling and knees bent at 90 degrees, hips also at 90 degrees.
Slowly extend one arm overhead and the opposite leg straight out, keeping the lower back pressed into the floor.
Return to the starting position with control, then repeat on the other side.
coachNote: A highly regarded core stability and rehab exercise — the goal is to move the limbs without letting the lower back arch off the floor.
tips: Keep the lower back pressed into the floor throughout.
Move slowly and with control, stopping if the back begins to arch.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back arch off the floor.
Moving too quickly, losing control of the core brace.
benefits: Excellent for core stability and rehab.
safetyNotes: Reduce the range of motion if the lower back arches.
Move slowly with full control.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, arms up, knees and hips bent at 90 degrees.
endingPosition: One arm and the opposite leg extended, back still flat.

name: Bird Dog
instructions: Start on all fours with hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips.
Extend one arm forward and the opposite leg backward simultaneously, keeping the back flat and hips level.
Hold briefly, then return to the starting position and repeat on the other side.
coachNote: A staple physical therapy exercise for training spinal stability and coordination between opposite limbs.
tips: Keep the back flat and hips level throughout.
Move slowly, avoiding any rotation of the torso.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate or tilt during the extension.
Arching the lower back excessively.
safetyNotes: Use a pad under the knees if on a hard floor.
Move slowly with full control.
startingPosition: On all fours, hands under the shoulders, knees under the hips.
endingPosition: One arm extended forward, opposite leg extended back.

name: Ab Wheel Rollout
instructions: Kneel on the floor holding an ab wheel with both hands, wheel positioned under your shoulders.
Roll the wheel forward, extending your body while keeping the core braced to resist the lower back from sagging.
Roll back to the starting position by contracting the abs.
coachNote: One of the most challenging and effective anti-extension exercises — start with a small range of motion and build up gradually.
tips: Keep the core braced throughout to prevent the lower back from sagging.
Only roll out as far as you can control the return.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back sag toward the floor.
Rolling out too far before building adequate core strength.
benefits: Trains anti-extension through a large range of motion.
safetyNotes: Use a pad under the knees.
Build up range of motion gradually to avoid lower back strain.
startingPosition: Kneeling, wheel under the shoulders.
endingPosition: Body extended forward, core braced.

name: Stability Ball Rollout
instructions: Kneel behind a stability ball, resting your forearms on top of it.
Roll the ball forward by extending your arms and body, keeping the core braced.
Roll back to the starting position by contracting the abs.
coachNote: A more accessible entry point than an ab wheel since the ball provides a larger, more stable contact surface.
tips: Keep the core braced throughout to prevent the lower back from sagging.
Only roll out as far as you can control the return.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back sag toward the floor.
Rolling out too far before building adequate core strength.
benefits: More accessible than an ab wheel rollout.
safetyNotes: Use a pad under the knees.
Build up range of motion gradually.
startingPosition: Kneeling behind the ball, forearms on top.
endingPosition: Ball rolled forward, body extended.

name: Barbell Rollout
instructions: Kneel on the floor holding a loaded barbell with small plates, hands shoulder-width apart.
Roll the barbell forward, extending your body while keeping the core braced.
Roll back to the starting position by contracting the abs.
coachNote: Similar to an ab wheel rollout but the longer bar can offer slightly more stability during the learning phase.
tips: Keep the core braced throughout to prevent the lower back from sagging.
Only roll out as far as you can control the return.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back sag toward the floor.
Rolling out too far before building adequate core strength.
benefits: Uses common gym equipment instead of a specialized wheel.
safetyNotes: Use a pad under the knees.
Build up range of motion gradually to avoid lower back strain.
startingPosition: Kneeling, barbell under the shoulders.
endingPosition: Body extended forward, core braced.

name: Renegade Row
instructions: Get into a high plank position with hands gripping dumbbells, feet spread wide for stability.
Row one dumbbell up to your ribs while resisting the urge to rotate your hips.
Lower the dumbbell with control, then repeat on the other side.
coachNote: A demanding combination movement — success is measured by keeping the hips square, not by rowing weight.
tips: Widen the foot stance for more stability.
Keep the hips as square to the floor as possible throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate excessively with each row.
Using a weight too heavy to control the anti-rotation properly.
benefits: Combines anti-rotation core training with a back and shoulder pull.
safetyNotes: Use hex dumbbells for stability on the floor.
Master a standard plank before attempting this.
startingPosition: High plank, hands on dumbbells, feet spread wide.
endingPosition: One dumbbell rowed to the ribs, hips square.

name: Weighted Plank
instructions: Get into a forearm plank position with a weight plate placed across your upper back.
Brace your core and hold the position, keeping the hips level.
Hold for the desired duration, breathing steadily throughout.
coachNote: Adding external load allows progressive overload once bodyweight plank holds of several minutes become achievable.
tips: Have a partner place and remove the plate safely.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the abs to keep the hips level.
commonMistakes: Adding too much weight too soon, causing the hips to sag.
Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
benefits: Builds significant core endurance and stability.
safetyNotes: Start with a light plate to assess tolerance.
Have a spotter assist with plate placement.
startingPosition: Forearm plank, plate placed on the upper back.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: Plank Walkup (Up-Down Plank)
instructions: Start in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders.
Lower down to a forearm plank one arm at a time, then push back up to a high plank one arm at a time.
Continue alternating the leading arm with each cycle.
coachNote: Transitioning between plank positions challenges anti-rotation stability even more than a static hold.
tips: Keep the hips as still as possible throughout each transition.
Alternate the leading arm evenly.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rock side to side during the transitions.
Rushing through the movement.
benefits: Builds anti-rotation core stability alongside upper body endurance.
safetyNotes: Master a static plank hold before adding transitions.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: High plank position.
endingPosition: Same position after cycling through a forearm plank.

name: Stir the Pot (Stability Ball Plank Circles)
instructions: Rest your forearms on top of a stability ball, feet spread wide behind you in a plank position.
Move your forearms in a small circular motion, as if stirring a pot, while keeping the hips and torso stable.
Complete circles in one direction, then reverse direction.
coachNote: The instability of the ball combined with the circular motion creates one of the most demanding core stability challenges available.
tips: Keep the hips and torso as stable as possible throughout the circles.
Start with small, slow circles.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag or sway excessively.
Making the circles too large before building adequate stability.
safetyNotes: Master a stability ball plank hold before adding circles.
Use a properly inflated, stable ball.
startingPosition: Forearms on the ball, plank position.
endingPosition: Same position, forearms moving in small circles.

name: Bear Crawl Hold
instructions: Get on all fours with hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips, then lift your knees an inch off the floor.
Hold this hovering position, keeping the back flat and core braced.
Hold for the desired duration, breathing steadily throughout.
coachNote: A demanding full-body isometric hold that trains the core, shoulders, and legs simultaneously without any equipment.
tips: Keep the back flat, avoid rounding or sagging.
Keep the knees hovering just off the floor throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rise too high, turning it into a downward-dog stretch.
Rounding the back.
safetyNotes: Use a pad under the hands and knees if needed.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: On all fours, knees hovering just off the floor.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: Overhead Carry
instructions: Press a dumbbell or pair of dumbbells overhead to full lockout, standing tall.
Walk forward for the desired distance while keeping the weight locked out overhead and the core braced.
Lower the weight with control once the distance or time is complete.
coachNote: Keeping a heavy weight stable overhead while walking demands total-body core bracing and shoulder stability.
tips: Keep the ribs down and core braced to avoid excessive lower back arching.
Take controlled, even steps throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back arch excessively.
Using a weight too heavy to maintain a stable overhead lockout.
benefits: Builds full-body core and shoulder stability.
safetyNotes: Master an overhead press before attempting the carry.
Choose a weight that allows a stable lockout throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, weight locked out overhead.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining the overhead lockout.

name: Plank Reach (Plank with Arm Extension)
instructions: Start in a forearm or high plank position, body in a straight line.
Extend one arm straight out in front of you, holding the position briefly while keeping the hips level.
Return the arm to the starting position and repeat with the other arm, continuing to alternate.
coachNote: Extending an arm removes a base of support, forcing the core to work harder to prevent hip rotation and sagging.
tips: Keep the hips as level and still as possible throughout.
Extend the arm fully for maximum challenge.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate or sag during the reach.
Rushing through reps instead of holding briefly at full extension.
benefits: Builds anti-rotation and anti-extension core stability.
safetyNotes: Master a standard plank hold before adding reaches.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Plank position, body in a straight line.
endingPosition: One arm extended straight out in front.

name: Superman
instructions: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended overhead and legs straight.
Simultaneously raise your arms, chest, and legs off the floor, contracting the lower back and glutes.
Hold briefly at the top, then lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A simple, no-equipment exercise for building lower back and glute strength, useful for balancing out heavy ab training.
tips: Squeeze the glutes and lower back at the top of each rep.
Keep the neck in a neutral position, looking at the floor.
commonMistakes: Overextending the neck by looking up too far.
Using jerky, fast movements instead of a controlled contraction.
benefits: Balances ab training with posterior chain strengthening.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled, avoid ballistic motion.
Stop if any lower back discomfort occurs.
startingPosition: Lying face down, arms and legs extended.
endingPosition: Arms, chest, and legs raised off the floor.

name: Back Extension (45-Degree Hyperextension)
instructions: Position yourself in the 45-degree hyperextension bench with hips against the pad and ankles secured.
Lower your torso forward by bending at the hips, keeping the back flat.
Raise back up to a straight line from head to heels by contracting the lower back and glutes.
coachNote: A staple lower back exercise — avoid hyperextending past a straight line at the top to protect the spine.
tips: Stop at a straight line at the top, don't hyperextend further.
Keep the movement controlled in both directions.
commonMistakes: Hyperextending the lower back beyond a straight line.
Rounding the back at the bottom of the movement.
benefits: Builds lower back, glute, and hamstring strength.
Simple to progressively overload with added weight.
safetyNotes: Adjust the pad and ankle position correctly before starting.
Avoid hyperextending the spine at the top.
startingPosition: Hips against the pad, torso bent forward.
endingPosition: Torso raised to a straight line from head to heels.

name: Weighted Back Extension
instructions: Position yourself in the 45-degree hyperextension bench, holding a weight plate against your chest.
Lower your torso forward by bending at the hips, keeping the back flat.
Raise back up to a straight line by contracting the lower back and glutes.
coachNote: Adding external load allows progressive overload once bodyweight back extensions become too easy.
tips: Keep the plate close to the chest throughout.
Stop at a straight line at the top, don't hyperextend.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight before mastering the bodyweight version.
Hyperextending the lower back beyond a straight line.
benefits: Allows progressive overload for the lower back and glutes.
safetyNotes: Master the bodyweight version before adding load.
Start with a light plate.
startingPosition: Hips against the pad, plate held on the chest, torso bent forward.
endingPosition: Torso raised to a straight line.

name: Swiss Ball Back Extension
instructions: Lie face down over a stability ball with your hips resting on top and feet anchored against a wall or held by a partner.
Lower your torso forward over the ball, then raise back up to a straight line by contracting the lower back.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The unstable ball surface adds a balance component to standard back extensions, without needing a dedicated machine.
tips: Stop at a straight line at the top, don't hyperextend.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
commonMistakes: Hyperextending the lower back beyond a straight line.
Losing balance on the ball.
benefits: Adds a balance and stability component to back extensions.
safetyNotes: Anchor the feet securely against a wall or with a partner.
Use a properly inflated, stable ball.
startingPosition: Lying face down over the ball, hips on top, feet anchored.
endingPosition: Torso raised to a straight line.

name: Prone Cobra
instructions: Lie face down with arms at your sides, thumbs pointed up, forehead resting on the floor.
Lift your chest, arms, and legs slightly off the floor, rotating your thumbs toward the ceiling.
Hold the position for the desired duration, breathing steadily.
coachNote: A gentle isometric exercise often used in posture correction and lower back rehab programs, less intense than a dynamic Superman.
tips: Keep the lift small and controlled rather than straining for height.
Focus on squeezing the shoulder blades together.
commonMistakes: Lifting too high and straining the neck.
Holding the breath instead of breathing steadily.
benefits: Gentle lower back and postural strengthening.
safetyNotes: Keep the range of motion small and controlled.
Stop if any discomfort occurs.
startingPosition: Lying face down, arms at the sides, thumbs up.
endingPosition: Chest, arms, and legs lifted slightly, held statically.

name: Banded Good Morning
instructions: Stand on a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart, looping the other end over your shoulders like a barbell.
Hinge forward at the hips with a soft knee bend, keeping the back flat.
Return to standing by driving the hips forward.
coachNote: A convenient, joint-friendly way to warm up or train the hip hinge and lower back pattern without a barbell.
tips: Keep the back flat throughout the hinge.
Only bend forward as far as your back stays flat.
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back.
Using a band too strong to control with proper form.
benefits: Joint-friendly lower back and hamstring activation.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Stop immediately if the back begins to round.
startingPosition: Standing, band looped over the shoulders and under the feet.
endingPosition: Torso hinged forward, back flat.

name: Reverse Plank
instructions: Sit on the floor with legs extended, hands placed behind your hips, fingers pointing toward your feet.
Press through your hands and heels to raise your hips until your body forms a straight line.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the hips elevated.
coachNote: This trains the posterior chain isometrically from the opposite orientation of a standard plank, balancing anterior and posterior core training.
tips: Keep the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Squeeze the glutes to help keep the hips elevated.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
Overextending the neck by looking up too far.
safetyNotes: Keep the wrists in a neutral, comfortable position.
Reduce the hold time if the shoulders fatigue.
startingPosition: Seated, legs extended, hands behind the hips.
endingPosition: Hips raised into a straight line, held statically for time.

name: Reverse Plank Leg Raise
instructions: Get into a reverse plank position with hips raised and body in a straight line.
Raise one leg straight up toward the ceiling while maintaining the hip height with the other leg and arms.
Lower with control back to the starting position, then repeat with the other leg.
coachNote: Removing one leg from the base of support significantly increases the stability and posterior chain demand.
tips: Keep the hips level and elevated throughout the leg raise.
Raise the leg only as high as you can without the hips dropping.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips drop as the leg raises.
Rushing through reps instead of controlling the raise.
benefits: Increased posterior chain and stability challenge.
safetyNotes: Master the standard reverse plank before adding leg raises.
Keep the wrists in a neutral position.
startingPosition: Reverse plank position, hips elevated.
endingPosition: One leg raised toward the ceiling, hips still elevated.

name: Kettlebell Windmill
instructions: Stand holding a kettlebell locked out overhead in one hand, feet turned slightly away from that side.
Keeping the arm locked out and eyes on the kettlebell, hinge sideways at the hips, reaching your opposite hand toward the floor.
Reverse the motion by driving through the hips to return to standing, then repeat before switching sides.
coachNote: A complex, highly technical exercise combining shoulder stability, hip hinging, and oblique control — start with just bodyweight or a very light weight to learn the pattern.
tips: Keep the overhead arm locked out and vertical throughout.
Keep your eyes on the kettlebell for shoulder stability awareness.
commonMistakes: Bending the overhead arm.
Rushing the pattern before mastering the hip hinge and shoulder stability separately.
benefits: Builds oblique, shoulder, and hip mobility and stability together.
safetyNotes: Learn the pattern with no weight or very light weight first.
Keep the overhead arm stable and locked throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, kettlebell locked out overhead in one hand.
endingPosition: Hinged sideways, opposite hand reaching toward the floor.

name: Turkish Get-Up
instructions: Lie on your back holding a kettlebell locked out overhead in one hand, same-side knee bent.

Follow the multi-step sequence to rise to standing — rolling to an elbow, then a hand, bridging the hips, sweeping the back leg through, and standing up — all while keeping the kettlebell locked out overhead.
Reverse the entire sequence with control to return to the starting lying position.
coachNote: One of the most complete total-body stability exercises in strength training — practice each step slowly without weight before adding load.
tips: Keep your eyes on the kettlebell throughout the entire sequence.
Move slowly and deliberately through each step, especially when learning.
commonMistakes: Rushing through the steps instead of controlling each phase.
Losing the overhead lockout position at any point.
benefits: Builds total-body strength, stability, and mobility simultaneously.
Highly regarded for shoulder health and core control.
safetyNotes: Learn the full sequence with no weight before adding a kettlebell.
Progress load gradually as competency improves.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, kettlebell locked out overhead in one hand.
endingPosition: Standing tall, kettlebell still locked out overhead.
